clue.text: A hot slice of tart epicure cooked to feed healthily

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the gathered letters are mixed into a new order
a slice is a small piece, so only one letter of the following word is taken, its opening one

explanation.surface: A gourmet's hot tart is baked to make a wholesome meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The food words all belong to the surface; every letter of A, HOT, T and EPICURE is reshuffled. This is a rare Chambers word, built from eutrophy, healthy nutrition.
explanation.definitionFit: Eutrophy means sound nourishment, and the verb formed from it means to supply such nourishment.

clue.text: Slough features in this involvement of Ed with Cissy

indicators.note: an involvement tangles things together, so the two names are mixed into one new word

explanation.surface: The English town of Slough appears in a story of Ed's affair with Cissy.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is not the Berkshire town but the cast-off skin of a snake, pronounced 'sluff'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecdysis is the moulting of skin or shell by snakes, insects and crustaceans, in which the old slough is shed.

clue.text: Turning point right within theme of discourse

indicators.note: within says one piece is placed inside the other

explanation.surface: A crucial moment in a debate, with the right view at its heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning point' suggests a crisis; read literally it is the line where the sun appears to turn back.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropics are the two latitudes where the sun stops and turns back at the solstices; the name comes from Greek for turning.

clue.text: Glutinous helping of chilly porridge served up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters run from bottom to top
a helping is a portion, so the letters are a portion lifted from the phrase

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A sticky spoonful of cold porridge put on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: The porridge words are all scenery; the answer itself describes cold porridge well.
explanation.definitionFit: Ropy describes something that forms sticky strings, like thick syrup or gluey liquid.

clue.text: Non-resident with state support, poorest struggling with ennui

indicators.note: something struggling twists about, so these letters wriggle into a new order

explanation.surface: A welfare claimant living elsewhere, the poorest of them battling boredom.
explanation.walkthrough: The poverty and boredom fit the picture of someone on benefits, which is the definition's own scene.
explanation.definitionFit: An out-pensioner draws a pension from an institution, such as Chelsea Hospital, without living in it.

clue.text: Old bungs foiled user opening special up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means reading from bottom to top
the jumbled letters open up the other piece by going into its middle
a foiled plan is thrown into disarray, so these letters are disarranged

explanation.surface: Old corks or stoppers that frustrated whoever tried to open a special bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: A bung suggests a stopper, matching the opening, but bung is old thieves' slang for a purse.
explanation.definitionFit: Bung was sixteenth-century cant for a purse, so old bungs are purses.

clue.text: To recap, with it Roman somehow encapsulated … his admired philosopher (12, two words)

definitions.text: To recap, with it Roman somehow encapsulated … his admired philosopher

indicators.note: to encapsulate is to enclose, so the jumbled letters go inside the phrase for recap

parts.note: in sum, a way of saying to sum up

indicators.note: somehow says the letters reach their form by some unstated rearrangement

explanation.surface: A Roman summing up his admiration for a favourite philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase is Cicero's, who said Plato alone was 'instar omnium', worth all the rest, so the Roman of the surface is the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Instar omnium is Latin for worth all of them, Cicero's tribute to Plato, the philosopher he admired.

clue.text: Chilled Scotch in Jock's bar?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Scots word for cold
second meaning: a Scots word for a weir or dam across a river

explanation.surface: Whisky served on the rocks in a Scottish pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotch is the Scots language, not whisky, and the bar is a barrier in a river, not a pub; Jock is a nickname for a Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: Scots uses the same word as an adjective for cold and as a noun for a dam or weir.

clue.text: Linking arms thus we each express nearness initially

definitions.note: a participle standing for a Scots preposition meaning between

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of each word in the run

parts.words: arms thus we each express nearness
parts.note: the first letter of each of the six words

explanation.surface: Two people walking arm in arm to show how close they are.
explanation.walkthrough: Linking arms is a phrase in the surface, but only 'Linking' defines; the word is Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Atween is a Scots form of between, the word that connects two things, as linking does.

clue.text: End of September? Hitter hit out

indicators.note: out as in out of order or out of place, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A batsman lashing out as the cricket season ends in September.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of September' suggests the letter R; the question mark warns it is the last date of the month instead.
explanation.definitionFit: September has thirty days, so its final day is the thirtieth.

clue.text: Big fish: company boss is about right

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the boss's title wraps around the next piece

explanation.surface: A business mogul, a 'big fish', is generally in the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big fish' reads as slang for an important person, which fits the company boss, but here it is a literal fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The cero is a large food and game fish of the mackerel family found in the western Atlantic.

clue.text: Bushwhackers may have these tin hats, battered

indicators.note: something battered is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
the letters of hats in a new order

explanation.surface: Men clearing scrub might wear dented tin helmets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tin hats' looks like a single phrase, helmets, but tin is its chemical symbol and only hats is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: A snath is the long shaft of a scythe, and a bushwhacker is a scythe-like tool for cutting undergrowth.

clue.text: Mayday, with character leading show, plump

indicators.note: the character at the front of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A distress call from a stout star of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: Plump is a verb here, to drop down heavily, not an adjective for stout.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives soss as a dialect verb meaning to fall or sit down heavily, which is to plump.

clue.text: Urgent — plump in the middle? See lens measurement

indicators.note: placing something in the middle of a word means it goes inside it

parts.note: to plump for something is to opt for it

explanation.surface: An urgent query about someone stout around the waist, followed by an eye test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plump' suggests fat, but here it is the verb, as in 'plump for', meaning choose.
explanation.definitionFit: A dioptre is the unit measuring the refractive power of a lens, used in spectacle prescriptions.

clue.text: E.g. Christian doctor, just as timely

parts.note: no later means just as soon

explanation.surface: A Christian physician who keeps his appointments punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' could be a first name, like the doctor's; here it means a believer in one god.
explanation.definitionFit: A monolater worships a single god, and a Christian is one example of such a believer.

clue.text: They ply their wares to men in camp — result's getting drunk

definitions.text: They ply their wares to men in camp

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of order, so these letters lurch into a new arrangement

parts.note: the letters of result's, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Traders selling to soldiers in camp, and the outcome is drunkenness.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue paints soldiers getting drunk on what the traders sell, which is exactly what sutlers supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: Sutlers were civilian merchants who followed an army and sold provisions and drink to the troops.

clue.text: Party provided warmth about start of evening

parts.note: so, as in 'so long as', means provided that

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for warmth closes round the following letter
the start of a word is its opening letter alone

explanation.surface: A party gave warmth as the evening began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warmth' here is warmth of temper, anger, not cosiness; the E goes inside it after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: A soirée is an evening party or social gathering, a word borrowed from French.

clue.text: Colts accepting start of training?

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the young animals hold the next letter

parts.note: a cade is a foal or lamb reared by hand

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter alone

explanation.surface: Young horses are taken on for their first lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: colts are also junior members of a team, and young recruits starting training are exactly that.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadets are young trainees, for the forces or police, much as colts are a club's junior players.

clue.text: Heat meat for cottage pie, setting aside first three quarters

indicators.note: setting something aside removes it, and first says the opening letter is what goes

parts.note: cottage pie is made with minced meat
three of the four compass points, the quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: Instructions for warming the filling of a cottage pie, a British dish of minced meat topped with mashed potato.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three quarters' sounds like a fraction of the meat, but quarters here are compass points. Heat is a verb: to make angry.
explanation.definitionFit: To incense someone is to make them furious, and to heat someone is likewise to inflame their temper.

clue.text: Falling backwards dumps catch

indicators.note: to fall backwards is to go the wrong way round, so the next word is read from its end

parts.note: to bin something is to dump it

explanation.surface: Someone tumbling backwards drops what they were meant to catch.
explanation.walkthrough: Catch is a noun here, the fastening on a door, and the word is Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: A snib is a Scottish word for a small bolt or latch that fastens a door or window.

clue.text: Lay about wandering male, minor luminary?

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for lay wraps around the other letters

parts.note: to lay money is to bet it

indicators.note: wandering letters stray from their places into a new order

explanation.surface: A roaming man who wagers might be a celebrity of the second rank.
explanation.walkthrough: A minor luminary sounds like a lesser celebrity; the question mark says take it literally, a small source of light.
explanation.definitionFit: A beamlet is a small beam of light, so it is a little light-giver.

clue.text: Canapé tastes of almond in the middle

indicators.note: the answer sits in the middle of the phrase, spanning its word breaks

parts.note: end of the first word, the second, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A party nibble flavoured with almond at its centre.
explanation.walkthrough: Canapé suggests a party snack, which suits the almond, but its original sense is the piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Canapé is French for a couch, and Chambers gives it in English for a kind of settee.

clue.text: Rolled up coat following guide

indicators.note: following places the word for guide after the word for coat

parts.note: an animal's coat is its fur

explanation.surface: A coat put away in a bundle after a guide's instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Furled describes a sail, flag or umbrella that has been neatly rolled and secured.

clue.text: Experience, taking in flash? One has no shorts!

indicators.note: to take something in is to enclose it, so the first word holds the second

parts.note: to see a thing happen is to experience it
a flash is a pool of water

explanation.surface: Life experience, with a dash of exhibitionism, from someone not wearing shorts.
explanation.walkthrough: Shorts are short syllables, not trousers. A flash in the sense of a small pool is a mostly British dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: A spondee is a metrical foot of two long syllables, so it contains no short syllables at all.

clue.text: Dénouement left out of drama, no longer available

indicators.note: out of here means taken out of the word, so one letter is removed

parts.note: a dish that is off the menu is no longer available

explanation.surface: A play's resolution was cut, so the play can no longer be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre words make one picture, but drama loses its L and the end phrase is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The payoff is the climax or resolution of a story, the point where everything is worked out.

clue.text: Banter (one might suppose) I introduced to restrain

indicators.note: something introduced to a word is put inside it

parts.note: to deter is to hold back

explanation.surface: A note on joking banter, with someone held back from joining in.
explanation.walkthrough: Banter is read as 'ban-ter', one who bans; the bracket admits this is not the real word. Someone on a diet bans certain foods.
explanation.definitionFit: A dieter forbids themselves fattening foods, so they could jokingly be called one who bans.

clue.text: Evergreen climbers from Sri Lanka and the States, one of them

definitions.note: plural: the genus name stands for its plants

parts.note: international vehicle registration for Sri Lanka, formerly Ceylon
Iowa, one of the States, by its postal abbreviation

explanation.surface: Climbing plants that stay green, found in Sri Lanka and in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One of them' points back to the States, so it means a single state.
explanation.definitionFit: Clusia is a genus of tropical American evergreen trees and shrubs, many of which climb or start life as epiphytes.

clue.text: Approach part of archipelago?

indicators.note: part of says only a section of the next word is wanted

explanation.surface: Sailing towards one island in a chain.
explanation.walkthrough: Approach looks like a verb for sailing near; it is the golf noun.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf, a chip is a short lofted shot played towards the green, a kind of approach shot.

clue.text: Old soldier, last promoted to lead 20's a slight one?

indicators.note: the final letter is promoted to the front rank, so it moves from the end to the start

explanation.surface: A veteran, the last of his unit, promoted to a command post.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on 20 down, BEAMLET: a smile is a slight beam, as when a face beams.
explanation.definitionFit: To beam is to smile broadly, so a smile is a small version of a beam on the face.

clue.text: It's imbibed by Rama possibly

indicators.note: what is imbibed is taken inside, so the god's name holds the little word
possibly says the result is only one arrangement the letters could take

explanation.surface: Describing a drink taken by Rama, a hero and avatar of the god Vishnu.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the letters build the word, and the sentence describes the drink a Hindu god might take.
explanation.definitionFit: Amrita is the drink of immortality in Hindu mythology, the nectar consumed by gods.

clue.text: Damage fine stone, scratching sign of love or concord

indicators.note: to scratch something is to strike it out, so the love symbol is crossed off the stone

parts.note: onyx is a fine banded stone
X is a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Scratching a precious stone ruins its value, whether it marks love or agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign of love' reads as a symbol on the stone, but it is the X of a kiss, deleted.
explanation.definitionFit: Harmony and concord both mean agreement, and both are also musical terms for pleasing combinations of notes.

clue.text: Heading heavenward, maid leaves glittering stake

indicators.note: in a down clue, heading heavenward means going upwards, read bottom to top
when something leaves a word, its letters are taken away

explanation.surface: A maid rising to heaven gives up her sparkling wager.
explanation.walkthrough: Maid, written upwards, is the first four letters of the sparkly word, and they leave.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker an ante is the stake each player puts in before the deal.

clue.text: Line fashioned with top style?

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape something new, so the letters are formed into another word

explanation.surface: A fashion question about a garment's cut, top-class style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Style' suggests fashion, matching 'fashioned' and 'top', but it means a stylus, a pointed writing tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A pointel is an old word for a pencil or stylus, and style is another name for a stylus.

clue.text: Person catching fish he skins

definitions.note: a clause describing one who peels, standing for the noun

indicators.note: to catch something is to hold it, so the person's abbreviation surrounds the fish

parts.note: per. is an abbreviation for person

explanation.surface: An angler who lands a fish then skins it himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the skinner an angler; the definition is simply anyone who peels.
explanation.definitionFit: A peeler is one who strips the skin or rind from something, which is what skinning means.

clue.text: Vacated theatre and left only half set?

indicators.note: keeping only half a word means its second half is dropped
a vacated building is emptied, so only the outside letters of the word stay

parts.note: the first and last letters of theatre

explanation.surface: An empty theatre and a stage left half-built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' looks like stage scenery, which suits the theatre, but it is a television set.
explanation.definitionFit: Tele is a short informal word for a television, and a television is often called a set.

clue.text: Mitre might be this indication of grade (12, three words)

definitions.text: Mitre might be this indication of grade

parts.note: surface reading: a bishop's tall hat as a badge of rank in the church
setter's reading: the five letters of mitre, rearranged, spell a word for worthiness, so mitre is one arrangement of that word; the whole phrase also names a ranked list

explanation.surface: A bishop's mitre as a sign of his rank in the church.
explanation.walkthrough: The mitre is not a hat at all: its letters are a reordering of MERIT, an 'order of merit'. The phrase itself means a ranking, which is the indication of grade.
explanation.definitionFit: An order of merit is a ranked list by performance, and also a decoration awarded for distinguished service.
